annotations.keyFindings: Fortnightly pharmacist calls were followed by more patients reaching a 25 percent dose reduction at six months (58 against 37 percent) and fewer leaving care (11 against 24 percent); pain interference did not change.
annotations.limitations: Uncontrolled before-after comparison in one clinic; how patients who left care were counted is not described; secular change in prescribing not addressed.
annotations.notes: Closest match to the Vellmoor pathway.

annotations.keyFindings: Among 212 adults who chose to taper, mean dose fell 41 percent over 12 months, pain interference improved from 6.8 to 6.1, and 19 percent paused or reversed the taper; depression predicted smaller improvement.
annotations.limitations: No comparison group; 14 percent missing at 12 months, mostly patients who stopped attending.
annotations.notes: Supplies planning values for dose change and missing data.

annotations.keyFindings: Emergency visits for overdose or withdrawal were 1.7 times as frequent in the two months after reductions above 20 percent per month; no excess after reductions of 10 percent per month or less; excess concentrated where no follow-up contact occurred within four weeks.
annotations.limitations: Dispensing data do not show consumption; confounding by the reasons for reduction.
annotations.notes: Supports emergency visits and overdose as balancing outcomes.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 27 studies, multidisciplinary support with frequent contact was associated with greater dose reduction and stable or better pain and function; only six studies reported overdose or emergency visits.
annotations.limitations: Only five studies had a concurrent comparison; taper success definitions too varied to pool; search ended in 2019.
annotations.notes: Argues for a continuous primary outcome rather than a success threshold.

annotations.keyFindings: Disengagement within six months was 31 percent beyond 60 km against 15 percent closer; interpreter need doubled disengagement; fortnightly telephone contact reduced it among distant patients.
annotations.limitations: Retrospective clinic data; reasons for leaving rarely documented; one service.
annotations.notes: Names the two predictors for the disengagement analysis.

annotations.keyFindings: An eight-item telephone withdrawal checklist agreed with in-clinic assessment (intraclass correlation 0.81), took about three minutes and showed symptom peaks two to five days after each dose step.
annotations.limitations: 84 patients in one service; not tested with interpreters or rapid tapers.
annotations.notes: Usable at the existing fortnightly calls.

annotations.keyFindings: Collaborative pharmacist and physician tapering in primary care was followed by more patients with a 30 percent reduction at 12 months (28 against 17 percent), with no difference in emergency visits.
annotations.limitations: Allocation by region; larger intervention practices; primary care patients rather than complex pain referrals.

claims.text: In a specialist pain clinic, 58 percent of patients reached a 25 percent reduction in daily dose at six months after fortnightly pharmacist calls were added, against 37 percent before.
claims.passage: 58 percent of patients reached a 25 percent reduction in daily dose at six months, against 37 percent before
claims.interpretation: Supports pharmacist support as the exposure of interest; uncontrolled, so a planning value only.

claims.text: Overdose or withdrawal-related emergency visits were more frequent after reductions of more than 20 percent per month, with no measurable excess after reductions of 10 percent per month or less.
claims.passage: After slower reductions of 10 percent per month or less there was no measurable excess.
claims.interpretation: Emergency visits and overdose belong in the protocol as balancing outcomes even for slow tapers.

claims.text: Patients living more than 60 km from the clinic left a supported taper about twice as often as those living closer.
claims.passage: Disengagement, defined as no contact for six weeks, occurred within six months in 31 percent of patients living more than 60 km from the clinic and in 15 percent of those living closer.
claims.interpretation: Distance and interpreter need should be recorded at entry and the disengagement analysis limited to them.

claims.text: Among adults who chose to taper in two pain clinics, the mean daily dose fell by 41 percent over 12 months.
claims.passage: Over 12 months, the mean daily dose fell by 41 percent.
claims.interpretation: Planning value for the primary outcome.

claims.text: An eight-item telephone checklist for withdrawal symptoms agreed well with in-clinic assessment.
claims.interpretation: Withdrawal can be measured at the existing fortnightly calls.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Pharmacist support during slow tapers was followed by more dose reduction and fewer patients leaving care in one before-after study (58 against 37 percent reaching a 25 percent reduction), and a two-clinic follow-up found a 41 percent mean dose fall with slightly better pain interference. Fast reductions carried an excess of overdose or withdrawal-related emergency visits that slow reductions did not. Distance and interpreter need predicted disengagement. No study had a randomised comparison, and success definitions varied too much to pool.
gradeRationale: Observational and before-after studies from single services, one review of mostly high-risk studies, and indirect primary care evidence; consistent in direction but at serious risk of bias from selection and loss to follow-up.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.
